comparison: Both strongly support the finding that sex-biased gene expression turns over quickly in somatic tissues and faster than in gonads (C2, C3, C71-C79). OpenEval provides detailed statistical validation while peer reviewers call this 'a fundamental advance' and 'convincing.'

Both support the resampling analysis showing faster turnover in somatic tissues (C84-C88). OpenEval validates the statistical methodology while peer reviewers accept this as part of the broader evolutionary dynamics finding.

Both strongly support the mosaic pattern finding - lack of correlation in sex-biased expression across organs within individuals (C4, C131, C132, C39). OpenEval validates the statistical analysis while peer reviewers highlight this as supporting 'a mosaic model' that challenges binary classifications.

Both support the visualization of individual-level variation showing mosaic patterns (C134, C135). OpenEval notes the heatmaps effectively demonstrate the mosaic nature while peer reviewers accept this as evidence for the broader mosaic model.

Both support the main conclusion about mosaic patterns and overlapping distributions (C7, C210). OpenEval notes this is well-supported by converging evidence but cautions about the normative claim; peer reviewers call it 'a fundamental advance.'

Both support the finding of overlapping distributions in somatic tissues versus separation in gonads (C35, C36, C122-C130). OpenEval validates the density distribution analysis while peer reviewers accept this as part of the mosaic pattern demonstration.

Both support the human GTEx data comparison (C5, C37, C38, C145-C150, C215). OpenEval notes significant data limitations while peer reviewer 2 acknowledges 'known confounding issues' but accepts the findings as they 'echo the trends seen with the much more rigorous mouse data set.'

Both support the variance analysis showing sex-biased genes are recruited from high-variance genes (C92-C95, C34). OpenEval validates the non-parametric methodology while peer reviewers accept this as part of the overall high-quality dataset without explicit discussion.

Both support the adaptive evolution findings from MK test analysis (C99-C106). OpenEval validates the statistical approach while peer reviewer 1 explicitly notes this as a strength; reviewer 2 accepts the finding but suggests 'a stronger modeling framework would have made these inferences more robust.'

Both strongly support the module-based turnover findings (C107-C119, C223). OpenEval validates the WGCNA methodology while peer reviewer 2 calls this 'a remarkable observation that could not have been predicted from previous knowledge.'

Both support conclusions about faster evolutionary change in somatic tissues (C220, C221). OpenEval synthesizes multiple lines of evidence while peer reviewers accept this as part of the fundamental advance in understanding sex-biased expression evolution.

Both support the identification of conserved epigenetic regulators (C165-C170, C224). OpenEval validates the stringent conservation criteria while peer reviewers accept this finding as part of the comprehensive analysis without explicit discussion.

Both evaluate the single-cell RNA-seq analysis with appropriate caution (C159-C161). OpenEval rates this as UNCERTAIN due to technical limitations while peer reviewer 2 acknowledges 'known confounding issues' but accepts the findings as supporting the broader trends.

Both strongly support the basic quantification of sex-biased genes across taxa and organs (C29, C30, C47, C48, C62, C64-C70). OpenEval validates the statistical methodology while peer reviewers praise the 'compelling quality and size' of the dataset and 'controlled sampling.'

Both support claims about novelty and methodological contributions (C174, C216-C218). OpenEval validates the uniqueness of the approach while peer reviewers call it a study that 'fills a gap' and note the SBI metric, though both OpenEval and reviewers question whether a new metric name was necessary.

Both support the organ-specificity and low conservation findings (C31-C33, C49-C50). OpenEval validates these with multiple lines of evidence while peer reviewers accept this as part of the high-quality dataset demonstrating rapid turnover.

OpenEval rates the adaptive evolution argument as UNCERTAIN (C183-C190), noting the evidence is circumstantial and alternative explanations not fully excluded. Peer reviewer 1 accepts that turnover is 'often accompanied by signatures of adaptive protein evolution' while reviewer 2 notes the evidence but suggests stronger modeling would improve robustness. Both show some caution about definitive claims.

OpenEval supports the X-chromosome enrichment analysis and mathematical reasoning (C51-C61). No corresponding explicit peer review evaluation found, though this is accepted as part of the comprehensive dataset.

OpenEval supports the experimental design and statistical methodology (C40-C46, C27). Peer reviewers praise the 'controlled sampling' and 'standardized conditions' that minimize confounders, aligning with OpenEval's validation of the methodological rigor.

OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN the interpretation of mouse vs. human differences (C203-C206), noting the explanations mix biological and methodological factors in ways difficult to disentangle. No corresponding explicit peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN the medical implications and extrapolations (C211-C214), noting these require caution and additional disease-specific evidence. No corresponding explicit peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval supports the theoretical context about sexual selection and cooperative breeding (C191-C202), though notes some speculation about female intrasexual selection. No corresponding explicit peer review evaluation found.
